procedural_history.originating_court: Commissioner of Central Excise, Rajkot (for Civil Appeal No. 6033/2009) and CESTAT (for Civil Appeal No. 5744/2011)
procedural_history.impugned_order: Order dated 17.03.2009 of the Customs, Excise & Service Tax, Appellate Tribunal West Zonal Bench at Ahmedabad in Appeal No.E/228, 240 and 241 of 2007 (for Civil Appeal No. 6033/2009) and an order dated 4.4.2010 of the Gujarat High Court (for Civil Appeal No. 5744/2011)
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: In Civil Appeal No. 5744/2011, the Gujarat High Court dismissed an appeal filed by the revenue against an order of CESTAT, holding that no question of law arose.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The Revenue appealed to the Supreme Court after the CESTAT order was upheld by the High Court. The Supreme Court dismissed both appeals.

issue.issue_text: Whether the demands raised against the assessee were barred by limitation.

facts: The tax authorities (Revenue) issued a demand for differential duty against the assessee beyond the normal one-year limitation period.
To justify using the extended period, the authorities alleged that the assessee had deliberately suppressed facts and made willful misstatements.
The dispute arose from how the assessee determined the assessable value of its goods, specifically concerning the inclusion of duty benefits from advance licenses.
law: The extended period of limitation under the proviso to Section 11A(1) of the Central Excise Act, 1944, can only be invoked if there is deliberate suppression of facts or willful misstatement by the assessee.

When a dispute involves the interpretation of legal provisions where two plausible views can co-exist, it is unjustified to invoke the extended period of limitation by claiming the assessee's view lacks bona fides.
application: The Court determined that the core of the dispute was a matter of legal interpretation, where two plausible views on the correct valuation could exist.
In such a situation of a bona fide interpretation dispute, the assessee's actions could not be considered a deliberate suppression of facts or a willful misstatement.
Since there was no tenable claim of suppression, the necessary conditions for invoking the extended period of limitation were not met.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the demands were time-barred because the revenue department was not justified in invoking the extended period of limitation. The Court held that a bona fide dispute over legal interpretation does not amount to suppression of facts.

issue.issue_text: Whether the assessee held a bonafide belief that it was correctly discharging its duty liability, thus negating any malafide intent or suppression of facts.

facts: The assessee determined its duty liability based on an interpretation of law established by a tribunal (CESTAT) in a previous case (IFGL's case).
This tribunal decision was later overturned by the Supreme Court.
The assessee had disclosed its pricing policy to the department through separate letters.
The assessee filed the required returns, including the value of 'deemed exports' within the value of 'domestic clearances,' as the return forms did not have a separate column for deemed exports.
The Revenue's own show cause notice acknowledged that the self-assessment procedure did not require an assessee to submit all contracts and invoices.
law: Under a self-assessment scheme, an assessee is responsible for determining their duty liability based on their own judgment in a bona fide manner.
A belief is not rendered malafide simply because it is later found to be legally incorrect by a higher court.

In cases involving disputes over the interpretation of legal provisions where two plausible views can co-exist, it is unjustified to allege a lack of bona fides to invoke an extended period of limitation.
An assessee can only be accused of suppressing facts that they were legally required to disclose.
application: The Court found the assessee's belief to be bona fide because it was based on a prevailing view taken by a tribunal at the time. The assessee could not have foreseen that this view would later be overturned by the Supreme Court.
The Court noted that the valuation issue was a complex matter of legal interpretation where two plausible views could exist, which supported the assessee's claim of a good faith belief.

The Court rejected the Revenue's argument of suppression of facts. It found that the assessee had disclosed its pricing policy and had correctly filed its returns by including deemed exports with domestic clearances, as there was no separate column for it.
The Court also pointed out that since the assessee was not required to submit all documents under the self-assessment scheme, the failure to do so could not be considered suppression.

The Court criticized the Revenue for taking a contradictory position by arguing that the tribunal's decision was irrelevant for determining the assessee's bona fide belief, while simultaneously relying on the same case for its arguments on the merits of the valuation.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court accepted the assessee's position, concurring with the tribunal's finding that the assessee held a bona fide belief that it was correctly discharging its duty liability. The Court concluded that the assessee's belief, though ultimately found to be incorrect, was not malafide, especially since it was based on a plausible interpretation of the law supported by a tribunal decision at the time. Therefore, there was no suppression of facts to justify invoking the extended period of limitation.

issue.issue_text: Whether a party is entitled to raise a point on appeal that was not pressed before the lower tribunal or incorporated in the memo of appeal.

facts: During oral arguments before the Supreme Court, the Revenue (the appellant) raised a point regarding the 'wrongful clubbing of deemed export clearances'.
This specific point had not been mentioned in the original show cause notice, the order of the lower tribunal, or the memo of appeal filed with the Supreme Court.
law: A party cannot be permitted to argue its case by going beyond the written pleadings it has filed.
A point cannot be resurrected or raised on appeal if it was not pressed before the lower tribunal or incorporated in the memo of appeal.
application: The Court noted that the main argument made orally by the Revenue was an issue that was absent from all its written pleadings and the lower tribunal's decision.
The Court found that even if the point had been made at the very original stage, the failure to press it before the tribunal or include it in the appeal memo meant it was abandoned.
Therefore, the Court determined that the Revenue was not entitled to raise this new point for the first time during oral arguments at the Supreme Court level.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the attempt to raise the new point, holding that a party is not entitled to argue an issue on appeal that was not pressed before the lower tribunal and was not included in the memo of appeal, as parties are bound by their written pleadings.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the demands raised against the assessee were barred by limitation.
appellant_arguments: The appellant (Revenue) argued that the demands were not barred by limitation, supporting the original Commissioner's order which had rejected the assessee's defense on this ground.
respondent_arguments: The respondent (assessee) argued that the demands were barred by limitation. This position was accepted by the lower Tribunal.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the assessee held a bonafide belief that it was correctly discharging its duty liability, thus negating any malafide intent or suppression of facts.
appellant_arguments: The appellant (Revenue) implicitly argued that there was suppression of facts and no bonafide belief, which would justify invoking the extended period of limitation.
respondent_arguments: The respondent (assessee) argued that they held a bonafide belief, submitting that they were never required to separately furnish details of clearances made to holders of advance licenses (deemed exports) as Form ER-1 did not specify this.

arguments.issue_text: Whether a party is entitled to raise a point on appeal that was not pressed before the lower tribunal or incorporated in the memo of appeal.
appellant_arguments: The appellant (Revenue) attempted to orally argue a new point concerning the 'wrongful clubbing of deemed export clearances under the details meant for domestic clearances', asserting their right to raise it before the Supreme Court.
respondent_arguments: The respondent (assessee) would have argued that the Revenue is not permitted to raise a new point that was not pressed before the Tribunal or included in the memo of appeal.

cases.case_name: Collector of Central Excise, Hyderabad Vs. M/s. Chemphar Drugs and Liniments, Hyderabad
cases.principle: Regarding the invocation of the extended period of limitation under Section 11A of the Act.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: An assessee's belief regarding their duty liability is considered bonafide, and not malafide, if it is based on a legal interpretation established by a judicial tribunal, even if that interpretation is later overturned by a higher court. Consequently, such a situation does not constitute suppression of facts, and any demand for duty is confined to the normal period of limitation.
obiter: When an issue of valuation is one where two plausible views could co-exist, it supports the finding of a bonafide belief on the part of the assessee.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The Court found that the demands for differential duty were barred by limitation because the assessee held a bonafide belief that it was correctly discharging its duty liability. This belief was considered reasonable as it was based on a view taken by a division bench of the Tribunal which held the field during the relevant period. The Revenue's failure to demonstrate any specific legal provision that required the assessee to make additional disclosures meant that the allegation of suppression of facts was untenable, and therefore the extended period of limitation could not be invoked.
legal_tests_applied: The determination of whether there was fraud, collusion, willful misstatement, or suppression of facts is a question of fact that depends on the circumstances of a particular case.

A belief held by an assessee regarding its duty liability is considered 'bonafide' if it is based on a plausible interpretation of the law at the time, particularly if that interpretation is supported by a prevailing decision of a judicial or quasi-judicial body like a Tribunal, even if that decision is later overturned.

To establish 'suppression of facts' for invoking the extended period of limitation, the Revenue must show that the assessee failed to disclose information that it was legally required to disclose under a specific provision or rule.
why_appellant_lost: The Revenue failed to prove suppression of facts, as its counsel was unable to show any specific provision or rule that required the assessee to make the additional disclosures that were allegedly withheld.

The Revenue's assertion of suppression was negated by the Court's finding that the assessee held a bonafide belief, which was supported by the fact that the valuation issue was complex and had two plausible co-existing views.

The Court held that the assessee's belief, even if ultimately found to be incorrect by a later Supreme Court judgment, could not be considered malafide because it was based on a Tribunal decision that was the prevailing law at the time.
why_respondent_won: The respondent successfully established that it held a bonafide belief that its method of determining assessable value was correct, as this belief was based on a view taken by a division bench of the Tribunal in another case (IFGL’s case) that held the field at the time.

The Court concurred with the Tribunal's finding that the respondent's belief was not malafide, stating, "The mere fact that the belief was ultimately found to be wrong by the judgment of this Court does not render such belief of the assessee a malafide belief particularly when such a belief was emanating from the view taken by a division bench of tribunal."

The allegation of suppression was further weakened by the fact, recorded in the show cause notice itself, that the assessee had submitted its pricing policy to the Revenue authorities from time to time.
As suppression of facts could not be established, the demands for duty were held to be time-barred, as they were raised beyond the normal one-year period of limitation.
policy_considerations: An assessee should not be penalized for holding a belief about its tax liability that is based on a prevailing judicial interpretation at the time, even if that interpretation is later overturned by a higher court. This provides a degree of legal certainty and fairness to taxpayers.

The burden of proving suppression of facts for the purpose of invoking the extended period of limitation lies squarely on the Revenue, which must demonstrate a clear and deliberate breach of a specific legal obligation to disclose information.
